title: Maestro HealthTech - time-to-first-token, credits & privacy constraints
summary: Discovery focused on PLG quickstart path (free credits, TTFT), plus evaluation of hosted vs private for PHI-like data. Customer cares about SSO, KMS keys, audit logs and predictable latency. Agreed next step: provide SOC2 + architecture note, provision credits and schedule 1-week pilot benchmark on hosted with canary to dedicated path if needed.
topics: Security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs
action_items: Sophie Martinez: Share SOC 2 + security pack, architecture note for VPC flow [2026-04-20]
Liam Chen: Run initial latency/cost estimate for Maestro's expected QPS and docs [2026-04-22]
Priya Kapoor: Share sample traffic shape and PII classification doc with Redwood [2026-04-21]
Ethan Walsh: Confirm internal list of stakeholders for private deployment review [2026-04-23]
next_steps: Provision 50k free-token credits to Maestro account (self-serve trial)
Schedule 60-minute pilot kickoff to deploy sample requests and measure TTFT (within 3 business days)
Exchange security docs and narrow privacy requirements for PHI handling
If hosted pilot looks good, scope Dedicated demo & pricing
transcript: [00:00] Sophie Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. I'm Sophie, AE on the Redwood Inference team. With me is Liam, our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:10] Priya Kapoor: Good — thanks. We're juggling a few things but excited to talk about how we can get quickly to a prototype with low-friction creds and then figure out the privacy stuff.

[00:22] Liam Chen: Awesome. Quick agenda: walk through PLG quickstart and TTFT (time-to-first-token), then hosted vs dedicated vs private options, security questions, and finish with pilot success metrics. Sound ok?
[00:33] Miguel Torres: Yep, that's perfect. Our immediate goal is to get internal stakeholders a demo within two weeks and show latency numbers against our threshold.

[00:44] Sophie Martinez: Great, low lift: we can provision trial credits so you can call the Redwood API in self-serve. Typical TTFT from sign-up to first successful inference is a day or less — often under an hour for engineers who can run a curl request, but depends on SSO/everything.
[00:58] Ethan Walsh: When you say hosted TTFT, are you talking about the public API, or some VPC flow for us? We can't send full PHI to a multi-tenant stack without controls.

[01:12] Liam Chen: Good question. Hosted means Redwood's hosted API. For PHI we usually recommend either Hosted with contractual controls + configured retention settings, or Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem) where the inference plane sits in your network. There's also Dedicated which is reserved GPU pools with isolation but still managed by Redwood. Each has tradeoffs on latency/cost and setup time.
[01:35] Priya Kapoor: Can you unpack Dedicated vs Private? Our security team says they want keys in our KMS, SSO, and audit logs pushed to our SIEM if possible.

[01:46] Liam Chen: Sure. Dedicated gives you tenant isolation and predictable throughput — we provision a pool for you. Private gives you a customer-managed control plane option: VPC peering, bring-your-own KMS/HSM integration, and tighter network controls. For the KMS requirement, Private offers direct KMS integration; Dedicated can support customer-managed keys via our enterprise contract in many cases, but we'll validate with the security team. Audit logs and tracer hooks are available in both, but Private has more flexible retention/location options.
[02:12] Miguel Torres: About TTFT — we want to show product folks we can get an end-to-end demo in under a day. How realistic is that given our SSO requirement?

[02:22] Sophie Martinez: For pure dev flow (no SSO), under an hour is common: sign up, get API key, run quickstart to generate text/embeddings. If you need SSO/SAML for corporate login that's a separate setup step and can add a few days. But you can still run the trial API keys while SSO is being set up — so the product demo can happen quickly with dev tokens.

[02:45] Priya Kapoor: Ok so we can run an internal demo using API keys while SSO is in parallel. What about data retention — we cannot have transcripts retained beyond 24 hours for certain data classes.

[02:58] Liam Chen: We have configurable retention policies. For hosted trials we can set aggressive retention or zero retention for sensitive fields, and we can provide attestations. For stricter needs, Private or Dedicated with on-prem options ensure logs never leave your network — that's what many health customers choose.
[03:18] Ethan Walsh: Any examples of customers doing on-prem because of PHI?

[03:22] Sophie Martinez: Yes, several. They start with hosted to validate model quality and then move to Private for production. It's a common path: quick PLG trial → pilot on hosted → dedicated reserved capacity or private for compliance.
[03:35] Miguel Torres: Regarding models, do you have recommended quantized variants that balance latency/cost? Our infra budget is constrained.

[03:44] Liam Chen: We curate model variants and have quantization profiles. Redwood Optimize suggests quantization levels by workload. For short chat-style requests you often get good cost-latency tradeoffs with 4-bit quantized variants — but we recommend running a small benchmark with your prompt set because results vary.
[04:02] Priya Kapoor: Benchmark — that's one of our asks. We'd like tail latency numbers and token cost per request for our typical prompts. Can you run that for our traffic shape?

[04:12] Liam Chen: Yes. If you share sample traffic and prompt distributions, we can run a hosted pilot and provide per-token cost breakdown and latency percentiles. We'll include concurrent QPS and sequence-length sensitivity in the report.
[04:30] Sophie Martinez: Action item — Priya, can you share a redacted sample and expected concurrency? We can provision credits and then Liam will run the benchmark.
[04:38] Priya Kapoor: I can share a redacted dataset, yes. We need to ensure redaction before sending.
[04:44] Ethan Walsh: On integrations: our infra sits in AWS — do you have VPC peering and private link options?

[04:51] Liam Chen: We support VPC peering and AWS PrivateLink for Private deployments. For Dedicated we can place endpoints in a dedicated VPC and configure peering. This is often part of the enterprise setup, not the self-serve trial.
[05:07] Miguel Torres: Pricing — how transparent is the cost model? We want token-based billing, but also an estimate for reserved capacity if we go Dedicated.

[05:15] Sophie Martinez: Hosted is token-based and we show token and latency breakdowns in the console. Dedicated is usually a reserved-capacity commit with a monthly fee — we'll provide an estimate based on your pilot numbers. We'll also show examples of cost savings from batching and KV prefix caching.
[05:31] Priya Kapoor: Caching — will that affect correctness? We have dynamic user prompts but some repeated prefixes.

[05:37] Liam Chen: Prefix/KV cache is safe for deterministic prefixes; you configure cache keys. The runtime has cache invalidation hooks and we can granularly control which endpoints use caching so it doesn't affect freshness for personalized content.
[05:49] Sophie Martinez: Quick note — sometimes transcript keyboards mis-parse 'KV cache' as 'key-v cache' — but yes, we support fine-grained controls.
[06:00] (laughter)
[06:04] Miguel Torres: Ok. On the security checklist: SSO (SAML/SCIM), SOC2 report, KMS integration, audit logs to Splunk, data residency in US/EU — can you provide those artifacts?

[06:16] Liam Chen: Yes, we'll share SOC2, our compliance matrix, and an architecture note describing KMS flow and audit log delivery. For Splunk ingestion we can push logs or provide a connector depending on your preferred path.

[06:30] Priya Kapoor: Also curious about rollout strategies — if we deploy Redwood in-prod what are your fallback policies? We want graceful degradation if a model variant fails or if capacity is constrained.

[06:41] Liam Chen: Redwood has routing policies and automatic fallback to compatible model variants or lower-cost tiers. You can configure canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a hosted backup region. For Dedicated we recommend a secondary pool as a fallback. We'll walk through runbooks in the pilot.
[06:58] Ethan Walsh: How do you handle KV cache warm-up? For cold-starts we see latency spikes.

[07:05] Liam Chen: We do continuous batching and pre-warming strategies; we also support explicit warm-up calls and persistent KV caches for repeated sessions. Cold-start latency is primarily model loading; we mitigate with pinned model instances for Dedicated.
[07:20] Sophie Martinez: For the pilot we'll recommend a small set of representative prompts and sequences so Liam can simulate warm and cold traffic and give you p95/p99 numbers.
[07:30] Miguel Torres: Sounds good. Any blockers we should flag now?

[07:34] Priya Kapoor: Our lawyers will want language around data retention and subprocessors; that's expected. Also, we need to confirm whether Redwood stores logs in cleartext or encrypted-at-rest with our KMS.

[07:47] Liam Chen: Hosted stores logs encrypted-at-rest and we can enable customer-managed keys under enterprise terms; for full KMS control Private is the right call. We'll include specifics in the pack.

[07:59] Sophie Martinez: Let's run through a proposed pilot timeline: day 0: provision trial credits and demo; day 1-3: run benchmark and share results; day 4: review with product and security; day 5: decide on Dedicated vs Private scoping. Is that acceptable?
[08:15] Priya Kapoor: Tight but doable if we get the credits and the bench details. We'll need someone from our security team to join the review on day 4.
[08:24] Miguel Torres: Who will be our main contact for the bench?
[08:27] Sophie Martinez: Liam will lead the benchmark and be the technical contact. You can loop in Ethan as the infra contact.
[08:34] Ethan Walsh: OK. Also, do you support function/tool calling or structured output? We have a pipeline that expects JSON responses sometimes.

[08:42] Liam Chen: Yes — Redwood supports structured output, function-style calls, and tool integrations. We have an SDK and REST endpoints; streaming responses are also supported for lower perceived latency in UI flows.
[08:55] Priya Kapoor: Any gotchas for streaming with our web app? We use long-polling and websockets in different parts.
[08:59] Liam Chen: Streaming is web-friendly; many customers use SSE or websockets. We'll include examples in the quickstart repo for your stack.
[09:08] Miguel Torres: Great. One last question: our legal team is cautious about subprocessors — do you publish a list?
[09:14] Sophie Martinez: Yes we publish a subprocessors list and provide contract addenda for certain requirements. We'll include that doc in the security pack.
[09:22] (brief pause)
[09:25] Priya Kapoor: Ok let's recap next steps before we finish — we need credits, security docs, bench, and a follow-up meeting. Anything else?
[09:34] Liam Chen: We'll also send a short runbook for pilot steps with exact curl commands and sample prompts so your engineers can get TTFT under an hour if they want to try immediately.
[09:44] Sophie Martinez: Perfect. I'll send the welcome email right after this call with the credits and links. Thanks everyone — we'll sync on the pilot kickoff calendar invite.
[09:54] Priya Kapoor: Thanks Sophie, Liam. Looking forward to seeing the bench results.
[10:00] Miguel Torres: Thanks all.
notes: Transcript includes some ASR artifacts; speakers occasionally overlap. Customer emphasizes PHI-like constraints; pilot to run on hosted first with ability to move to Dedicated or Private for compliance. Agreed rough timeline for a 1-week pilot and SOC2/security pack exchange.
